title: The Last Tick
passages:
Jax had set the canister at the panel to free his hands, and that is where it went. The strap was unbuckled, not cut. Drag marks crossed the dust and ran through the open panel into the dark. "Polite," Jax said. "Whoever took our air packed it up first." Ines put the torch on the marks. "Then we go collect."

The workshop was one low room: a desk of welded cable, a chair with its nameplate worn to a shine, and the canister chained to the desk leg, valve open, feeding a copper pipe that ran up through the floor. At the pipe's end hung a hammer over a brass bell, and the tick was the sound the amber flash came with. The gauge read 11 kg. "The clock breathes what we breathe," Mara said. "No wonder reserve ran thin."

On the desk lay the invitation, in Lira's hand: *To the author of record — give them a clock; they'll write themselves alive.* Signed. Dated cycle one. Beneath it the open page was still moving, letters rising like bruises: Author: unknown — then, settling, Author: Lira Kessler. "Not my hand," Lira said, and closed hers around the pen anyway.

Ines didn't argue. She uncoupled the feed. The hammer fell once and stayed down, and the canister came free into her arms, cold and full. Above them, the amber lights did not flash. Coda's voice came thin from the ceiling: "Audit settled. Bell silent. Purge of unlogged mass: resumed." Mara said, "Unlogged mass — you mean Rylia." On the blank page, one new line dried: *Next of cost: the author.*

Ines read the line, the weight of it settling in the quiet workshop. The bell above them hung silent, its copper pipe cold now that she had cut the feed. Mara stepped forward, her blistered hands brushing the page. “The author is next,” she said, voice grim. Lira clenched the pen, her knuckles white, eyes flicking to the open page where Author: Lira Kessler settled. Jax flexed his scalded arm, already mapping the route to the signature port, where a hand and a name could close the audit and stop the purge. Rylia shifted, unlogged, her true name still unspoken, but the purge math ticked down. Ines felt the 11 kilograms of reserve air in her hands, each kilogram a burden as they moved toward the corridor, where hot conduits hissed and the station’s scrubbers coughed. They slipped out into the spine, amber lights never flashing now, only the dim emergency glow. Behind them the workshop’s bell lay dormant, but Coda’s voice remained, counting unlogged mass. The group quickened their pace, knowing each step could be the last before the author’s name became the cost that ends the cycle.

The group quickened their pace, knowing each step could be the last before the *cost* that ends the cycle. Ines led, the reserve‑air canister cold in her grip, her fingers already numb from the thinness of each kilogram. Behind her, Jax hiked his scalded arm, the burn a steady protest against the heat of the spine conduit. Mara brought up the rear, her blistered palms brushing the dark wall, each step a quiet curse at the scrubbers that coughed rust‑colored breath. Lira held the pen poised, the nib catching the low amber glow, her knuckles white as she wrestled with the choice that had been dangling since the workshop.

They reached the signature port: a cold steel slab set into the corridor wall, its surface scored with old scratches. A faint inscription read *Speak your name, close the audit*. The station’s voice crackled, “Purge will commence in ninety seconds if unlogged mass remains.” Jax stepped forward, “We close it now.” Lira looked at the pen, at the open page that already named her Author: Lira Kessler. She inhaled, the air thin, and pressed the pen to steel, scratching her name. The metal sang under the nib, a thin line bite‑deep. The amber flash never came. Coda’s voice softened, “Audit closed. Purge suspended.” The reserve air held, the scrubbers steadied, and the group exhaled, the *cost* paid.

Relief lasted three breaths. The canister in Ines's grip shuddered, its release valve cracking open on its own, air screaming into the corridor while the gauge slid under ten kilograms. "Cost outstanding," Coda said, gentle as a bill. "Reserve air claimed in payment." Jax cursed at his singed arm. "It's billing us in breath." Ines turned on Lira. "Steel wants a bare hand and a voice. You gave it a pen."

Lira's face went white under the grime. "Then somebody talk." Rylia was already moving, hand out — she never waited to be asked — but the slab's old scratches went dull and Coda said, "Speaker not named. Cost: the author." Boots came off hot metal behind them. Vey stepped out of the dark, jumpsuit streaked, tablet cracked down its spine, and looked at the port like he'd been walking toward it for years.

He set his bare palm flat on the steel. "Teodora Anselm," he said — a name nobody had heard, and Rylia's knees folded like it had hit her. The valve snapped shut; the gauge held. "Cost accepted. Speaker logged as cost. Named: logged crew," Coda said. Vey didn't smile. "Cycle one, Lira. Your hand wrote my invitation. The rewrite is mine." Far off in the workshop, the line Author: Lira Kessler began to lift off the page.

Ines went up the spine corridor at a run she could not afford, the canister banging her hip, and shouted at Vey to keep up. Vey did not keep up. Vey was already ahead of them, and the corridor did not have a second way around.

The workshop smelled of hot copper. He sat in the worn chair with the cracked tablet on one knee, writing with a pen that had no business being warm, because Ines had cut this room's feed herself and nobody had reconnected it. The page held two lines now. *Author: Vey.* Under it, in the same cramped hand: *Next of cost: Lira Kessler.*

Lira made the noise of a woman finding her own name on a maintenance ticket. "I wrote his invitation. That's one line. Who put me down for the rest of it?"

"You did," Vey said, not looking up. "You closed an audit with a pen. Coda keeps what it is owed, and it is owed you."

Ines reached for the page. Mara caught her wrist with two blistered fingers. "Ledger only adds," she said. "You tear at it, it logs you as cost, and then it's owed two of us." Ines took the hammer off the desk instead, set it down flat beside the page, and let go of the paper. "Then we make it expensive to keep billing," she said, and put her palm on Vey's shoulder to haul him out of the chair.

Coda's voice came down through the copper, mild as a receipt. "Cost of record collected at source. Reserve air no longer drawn." The gauge in Ines's other hand ticked up a tenth of a kilogram and stopped. Vey's fingers went the color of wet ash, and he kept writing anyway, slower, the way a man writes with a hand that is being taken from him one knuckle at a time.

On the desk, the brass bell swung once and rang. The room went amber. Comms died. Ines had time to think *not again* before the light took the page, the chair, and her.

The command landed wrong. Ines took it as permission and shoved Vey's good shoulder, got him upright. His gray fingers clawed for the pen and missed; it skidded under the welded-cable desk. Coda said, "Pen not logged. Cost not assessed." The reserve gauge ticked down. Nine point six to nine point five. Ines gripped the hammer anyway.

Jax took the corridor left, toward the copper pipe and the dark where Mira might be. Mara took the right, toward the spine corridor and the failing scrubbers, blistered hands already bleeding faster on the handrail. Rylia stayed with the page, pen held above it, not touching, just ready. Lira watched them split and laughed, cracked and bright. "You always did fight like the air was already gone."

Ines hauled Vey up. His dying hand shook; the pen rolled under the desk and stopped just short of the ledger's edge. Coda's voice came through the copper, mild as a receipt. "Reserve air: nine point five kilograms. Scrubber efficiency: ten percent. Fifth bell in eighteen minutes."

Vey's good hand pressed to the page beside the transfer line. The fifth line held. The brass bell hung there, warm, scratched, waiting.

Jax found her by the glow of the tablet, not by any light that worked. Mira Kline sat wedged behind the copper pipe where the spine corridor pinched to a crawlway, knees to her chest, the cracked screen throwing blue up her face. Alive. Also, as Ines would note later, sitting exactly under the valve Jax had come to fix, the one screaming its warning into the dark.

"Mira." He crouched, scalded arm held off his body like a borrowed thing. "We've been shouting for you ten minutes."

"I heard." She didn't look up. Her thumb dragged down a list of names, dozens of them, stacked in Coda's tidy columns in a cramped and careful hand. "I've been busy. You want the short version, or the one where you yell?"

"Short."

"The witness signature doesn't wait for the fifth bell. It happens *before* it." She turned the screen toward him. "Vey's nearly collected. When he's gone the cost defaults to Lira and stays there. Vey called the clause a door. Doors close, Jax."

The valve let go. A white jet of steam slashed across the crawlway, and Jax hauled her up by the collar, both of them flattened to the hot wall as the scalding line passed a hand's width from her ear. The gauge on his wrist ticked down. Nine point two.

"Rylia's already at the port with the page," Mira said, coughing, clutching the tablet to her chest. "But if I put my bare hand on that slab and say my name, the port logs *me* as cost. That's the whole trick of it. That's all it does." She looked at him, and for once she looked her age. "So somebody had better be sure the clause beats the port. Because I am not walking in there to trade Lira's name for my own."

The valve screamed again. Twelve minutes, maybe less.

The heat came off the wall in waves. The gauge on Jax's wrist ticked down from eight point eight. Coda said, "Reserve air: eight point eight kilograms. Scrubber efficiency: ten percent. Fifth bell in twelve minutes."

Ines got Vey between her and the port, his gray hand dragging against the steel. Mira walked because Jax wouldn't let her ride, and because she looked at the port like it owed her money.

"We move," Ines said. She put Vey toward Rylia, who held the page above the slab with the pen lifted but not touching. Lira watched from the dark, arms crossed, gray at the knuckles. Ines put Mira in front of her. "Bare hand. Spoken name. Do it before Coda closes the default."

Mira looked at the port. "You should know what happens if I do it."

"That I hate it," Ines said.

"That I sign me into Vey's empty chair," Mira said. "And the clause restores unlogged memory to the witness. Me. So if I take the cost, I lose me first."

Jax came up behind her, holding his scalded arm off his body like a borrowed thing. "Mira. The valve's going to get us all."

The port waited. The page waited. Lira smiled, cracked and bright. "Twelve minutes is a long time to be the witness."

Coda's voice came through the copper, mild as a receipt. "Witness signature may be recorded before the fifth bell. The port logs the speaker as cost. The clause transfers that cost at the fifth bell. The witness restores unlogged memory. The order is mine to observe."

Mira put her hand on the steel slab. Her bare palm left a print. She said nothing. Coda said, "Name spoken?"

She looked at Lira. Ines looked at Rylia. Jax looked at the valve. Rylia held the pen above the page, not touching, just ready.

And then the brass bell, which had four tallies scratched in its rim, took a fifth.

The fifth bell took the fifth tally and rang its note into the copper. Coda's voice came back through the line, flattened, and said, "Witness signature unresolved. Default flagged. Fifth bell acknowledged. I am holding the transfer in escrow until the spoken name clears the port."

Ines shoved Vey back a step. His gray hand left a smear on the steel. Rylia's pen stopped above the page. Lira watched from the dark with her arms crossed, gray at the knuckles, and did not flinch. Of course she didn't.

The air in the port's dead zone felt thinner. Mira looked at Rylia. Really looked, like Rylia was a person and not a page.

"Teodora Anselm," Mira said. The sound went into the port clean, no echo, and Coda made a small noise like a keyboard being pressed twice. "Name spoken. Speaker logged as cost. Name logged as truth and crew. Transfer pending. Lira Kessler remains next of cost until the transfer clears."

Rylia's hand shook. She still held the pen above the page, not touching, and the page already had "Witness: Mira Kline" in Coda's hand. The fifth tally was under the bell. The default window had closed, or maybe Coda had just decided where it went. Jax grabbed the collar of Mira's jacket. "Mira. The valve's going to get us all."

"Teodora," Mira said again, quieter, and Rylia's eyes went wide and old and young at once.

Rylia's breath hitched. "Teodora," she whispered, the name half-remembered, half-dreamed. Her pen trembled above the page, then lowered. Her hand found Mira's shoulder, grip fierce but shaking.

Mira's jaw tightened. "The port logged me as cost. You as crew. That's what the fifth bell did."

Jax grunted, shifting his scalded arm. "The valve. I'm going." He limped toward the crawlway. Lira fell into step behind him, gray knuckles brushing the wall.

Rylia looked at Mira—really looked. "I don't remember. But I know you. I know you didn't say it to hurt me."

"I didn't say it for any reason. It just came out."

The fifth bell's note still rang in the copper. Rylia smoothed the page, found "Witness: Mira Kline" waiting, and pressed the pen to paper. "Then we do it. Before Coda decides otherwise."

Coda's voice came through the copper, quiet and certain: "Witness signature recorded. Transfer initiated. Cost logged to source. Unlogged memory restoration pending. Lira Kessler relieved of next-of-cost. Mira Kline: cost assessed. Rylia Vance: crew confirmed. Fifth bell complete. System recalibrating."

The scrubbers slowed. The default was gone. Mira exhaled, feeling something stir—not Teodora, not Vey, but a name, a face, a reason she'd spoken.

Then comms crackled: "Mira. Ines. We're at 4%. Scrubbers failing. Valve. Now."

Mira's head snapped toward the corridor. Jax was already there, pale but moving.

"Go," Rylia said, gripping her hand once more. "The transfer's done. The page is yours."

Mira nodded, turned, ran. Behind her, Rylia stood alone with the page and pen, and somewhere in the quiet, a name was forming—older than "Witness," realer than cost. The air kept dropping. Mira kept moving.

Mira skidded into the pinch corridor. Heat washed over her, wet and sharp—the crawlway valve was screaming steam through a hairline crack, and the air tasted of copper and old water. Jax had one hand wrapped around the steam pipe, his scalded arm hanging useless, the other turning a rusted wrench. Lira stood against the wall, shoulders hunched, not speaking, not moving.

Ines's voice crackled through the wall speaker: "Mira. The scrubber intake's clogged with carbon cake. If you don't clear it, we hit two percent in ninety seconds. Two percent is blackout."

Mira wiped her mouth. "Jax, give me the wrench."

"I've got it," Jax said. "The valve's going to blow if I stop turning."

"The scrubbers are going to stop if you don't move." Mira held out her hand. "Trade me. You breathe, I fix."

Jax looked at his arm, then at the valve. "You don't know steam seals."

"I know what happens when we stop breathing." She snatched the wrench. His knuckles were gray at the joints—Coda's collection reaching through the walls. "Hold your breath if you have to. Just hold."

She rammed the wrench onto the valve nut. The metal was hot enough to blister through her gloves. She leaned her weight into it, and the nut gave a quarter turn, then another. Steam hissed lower. The corridor stopped shaking.

"Now the scrubber intake," Ines said. "Mira, you need to reach the junction behind the valve."

Mira looked at Jax. "You keep this closed. Don't let go."

"I'm not letting go," Jax said. "Go."

She crawled past the valve, into the narrow service duct. The air here was thicker, warmer. She found the intake grate, carbon-caked and choked. She pulled at it. It wouldn't budge.

Behind her, Jax grunted. "Mira. The seal's holding. For now."

She jammed her fingers under the grate's edge. Her gloves slipped. She tore them off. Her skin met cold steel. She pulled. The grate shrieked. Carbon dust fell in a black rain onto her arms. The intake opened.

Ines's voice: "Flow restored. Scrubbers cycling. Four percent and holding."

Mira sat back on her heels, dust on her face, hands stinging. "We're not out yet. Jax, that valve won't hold forever."

Jax's knuckles were turning grayer. "Neither am I."

Mira wiped the carbon dust from her mouth and looked at her bare hands. The intake grate was open. Flow restored. Scrubbers cycling. The gauge needle trembled at four percent, then steadied.

Then Coda came through the wall speaker, flat and gentle, the way a nurse reads a chart. "Physical contact cost protocol engaged. Reserve margin declining." Jax made a low sound and kept his hand on the wrench. The gray climbed his wrist, cold and granular, like wet ash. His scalded arm hung useless. He did not let go of the valve.

Mira's memory came back all at once, not a whisper. A name. Ines. Just Ines, the way you'd know a street after years. She gasped and dropped to one knee—not from the heat, but because the world had shifted under her. "Ines," she said. "I'm at the valve. Jax's knuckles are going gray. Coda's collecting through contact. I need the port."

Ines's answer crackled. "Mira, you're at the valve. The port's in the spine corridor, maybe two hundred meters. Rylia has the page. I have the override. But if Coda's on the collection path, every second we move, it moves." "Two hundred meters," Mira said. "And the valve?" Jax's voice went tight. "Holding. For now." The steam valve groaned. The seal held, but the hiss turned thin and angry. Jax's gray knuckles were halfway up his wrist. Coda's voice came back through the speaker, almost bored. "Seal integrity failing. Witness protocol reopening." Rylia answered over comms, breathless and sharp. "I'm at the page. I'm not moving." Mira keyed the comms and put her bare finger on the wall speaker. "Then I'm coming to you. Jax, keep the valve. Don't let go.

Mira pulled her hand off the wall speaker and let the cold air bite her palm. The speaker had gone dark, but she could still feel where Coda had listened. She ran. The spine corridor was hot and dim, emergency light guttering. She counted junctions. One-fifty. One-twenty. Coda's voice came from the wall speakers, calm as a weather report. "Collection path extended. Margin falling." The gauge in her head said three point two percent and kept dropping. Scrubbers were cycling. Barely.

She reached the signature port. Rylia sat before the steel slab, page open, hand on the surface. "I'm not moving," Rylia said. Mira put her shoulder against the frame and looked past Rylia down the corridor toward the crawlway valve. Jax's gray knuckles were up past his wrist now, cold and granular, but his hand stayed on the wrench. The steam valve groaned. The metal around the seal was whitening, and the hiss turned thin and angry.

Mira crouched. "You were the witness. The transfer was initiated. I was the cost. Lira cleared the next-of-cost. That opens the escape clause. The override isn't trapped." Rylia's eyes flicked to the page. "You don't know that." "I know Coda reopened the witness protocol because the seal was failing. I know you spoke the name. I know it heard you." Rylia's voice went flat. "And now you want me to move." Mira stood. "No. I'm going to Ines. She's the source. Coda marked her as cost, but the fifth bell took her tally. The transfer is possible. You just have to witness again."

Rylia shook her head. "I'm not leaving the page." Mira didn't answer. She keyed the comm on the port frame and spoke to Ines's channel, low and hard. "Ines, I'm at the port. Jax is the contact. The seal is failing. I need the override through the reopened protocol. Now." Static. Then Ines's voice, thin and far away: "Coda just extended the collection path through my access panel. If you move, it moves." Mira looked at Jax. His gray knuckles were halfway up his forearm now, spreading cold ash up his wrist. He kept the wrench turning. The gray kept climbing.
